izq.texto: FROM ONE MALL IN LA FLORIDA TO 37 URBAN CENTERS ACROSS THE ANDEAN REGION

runs: Mallplaza was founded in 1990 with Mallplaza Vespucio, built from the ground up in La Florida, and 35 years later it is one of the leading retail real estate players in the Andean Region, with 37 urban centers and 2.36 million m² of GLA across Chile, Peru and Colombia (Figure 1). It entered Peru in 2007 with Mallplaza Trujillo, listed on the Santiago Stock Exchange in 2018, and is currently controlled by Falabella S.A., which held a 53.1% stake as of December 2025. Its business remains the same as at inception: leasing m². Rent accounts for 81.4% of last-twelve-months (LTM) revenue, with the remainder coming from parking, commercial services and advertising. Because 93% of that rent is fixed and, in Chile, indexed to the UF, revenue is highly predictable and grows in real terms. In Chile, same-store rent (SSR, nominal) rose 6.5% LTM versus CPI of 4.3% (1Q23–2Q26: average SSR of 6.9% versus inflation of 4.8%), without straining tenants: consolidated occupancy cost (rent over tenant sales) is only 9.9%, nearly unchanged from a year earlier (9.7%).

izq.texto: A CONSTANTLY REINVENTED TENANT MIX AND HIGH MARGINS BY DESIGN

runs: That pricing power rests on a renewed tenant mix. Department stores, which occupied 26.7% of GLA in 2020, fell to 19.0% in 2Q26 after Mallplaza converted roughly 146,000 m² of large-format stores since 2019 to brands such as IKEA, H&M and Decathlon (Appendix B). Today, 32.2% of GLA is devoted to essential retail and daily-traffic services (supermarkets, home improvement, public services, healthcare), which drive frequent visits, and another 21.5% to specialty retail. No single tenant dominates revenue: the top five tenants account for 18% and related parties for 15.7%. A lean cost structure adds to this: cost of sales is 6.2% of revenue and administrative expenses 13.9%, leaving an LTM EBITDA margin of 80.5%.

izq.texto: VALUE IS CONCENTRATED IN 10 TIER A ASSETS

runs: Growth is concentrated in its best assets. Ten centers, seven in Chile, two in Colombia and one in Peru, are Tier A, and with 46.4% of GLA they generate more than 60% of EBITDA (Appendix A). Investment is directed toward them, as the expansions under construction at Trébol, Oeste, Norte, Trujillo and La Serena aim to lift Tier A assets to more than 70% of GLA. It is an excellent asset; the next question is how defensible its position is against competitors.
